paper.title: An Exact Semidefinite Lift of a, Nonspectrahedral Hyperbolicity Cone
paper.html:
Abstract

We construct an exact semidefinite lift of the explicit nonspectrahedral hyperbolicity cone in twenty-three variables defined in the companion paper. The lift is a homogeneous real symmetric pencil of size 100 with 307 auxiliary variables and represents the entire closed cone, including every point with singular X. Thus, although this cone has no semidefinite representation in its original coordinates, it admits one when auxiliary variables are allowed. The stated sizes are not claimed to be minimal.

1 Introduction

Let Sn denote the real symmetric n×n matrices. A spectrahedron is a set defined by a finite affine linear matrix inequality; a spectrahedral shadow is a linear projection of such a set. Thus auxiliary variables may make a semidefinite representation possible even when no representation exists in the original variables. We study this distinction for one explicit hyperbolicity cone.
For a homogeneous real polynomial p with p(e)>0, hyperbolicity with respect to e means that t↦p(te−x) has only real roots for every x. We use the closed-cone convention
K(p,e)={x:every root of t↦p(te−x) is nonnegative}.
In particular, zero roots are allowed.
The convexity of hyperbolicity cones goes back to Gå rding [G\r ar59]. In three variables, the Helton–Vinnikov theorem yields definite symmetric determinantal representations, and hence spectrahedral cones [HV07; LPR05]. Allowing auxiliary variables leads to a broader representation question. Netzer and Sanyal proved semidefinite liftability when every nonzero boundary point is a smooth point of the defining hyperbolic polynomial [NS15]. More recently, Scheiderer obtained second-order cone lifts under a Nash-smooth boundary hypothesis [Sch25]. Our result instead concerns an explicit cone and gives its lift by a bounded-degree algebraic construction.

1.1 The cone and the main result

For y=(y1​,y2​,y3​)∈R3, define
Q(y)=​y12​+y22​−y1​y2​−y1​y3​​−y1​y2​y22​+y32​−y2​y3​​−y1​y3​−y2​y3​y32​+y12​​​.(1)
The associated biquadratic form zTQ(y)z is the coefficient-one Choi–Lam form [CL77, Section~4]. For a∈R, r∈R3, and T∈S3, set
Φy​(ar​rTT​)=(tr(Q(y)T)−Q(y)r​−rTQ(y)aQ(y)​).(2)
This is a linear map from S4 to itself for each fixed y. On the space V=S4×S4×R3, define
p(X,Z,y)=det((detX)Z−Φy​(adjX)),e=(I4​,I4​,0),(3)
where adjX denotes the classical adjugate. Each matrix entry inside this determinant is homogeneous of degree five, and p(e)=1; hence p is homogeneous of degree twenty. We write K=K(p,e). The slice representation in Section 2 will in particular verify that p is hyperbolic with respect to e.
Identify V with R23 by listing the upper triangular entries of X, then those of Z, each in lexicographic order of (i,j), followed by y1​,y2​,y3​.
Theorem 1.1.
There exist fixed matrices A1​,…,A23​,B1​,…,B307​∈S100 such that, for every x=(X,Z,y)∈V,
x∈K⟺there exists v∈R307 with ν=1∑23​xν​Aν​+j=1∑307​vj​Bj​⪰0.
The equivalence holds on the entire closed cone, including points with singular X.
The sizes in Theorem 1.1 are explicit bounds, with no minimality assertion. The matrices are specified by a finite coefficient rule in Section 4.
The cone in (3) was constructed in the companion manuscript [Ope26], whose Theorem 1.1 proves that it has no homogeneous semidefinite representation in its original twenty-three coordinates. This also excludes affine representations. Indeed, if a cone containing 0 equals {x:A0​+L(x)⪰0}, where L is linear, then A0​⪰0. For each point x of the cone and t>0, we have A0​/t+L(x)⪰0; letting t→∞ gives L(x)⪰0. Conversely, L(x)⪰0 implies A0​+L(x)⪰0; thus the same cone has the homogeneous representation L(x)⪰0. We use the companion result only for this comparison: the proof of Theorem 1.1 below is self-contained. The companion also establishes hyperbolicity and, in Proposition 3.2, describes the part of K with X≻0. Our slice calculation recovers those two facts as part of the lift construction.

1.2 Proof strategy

The starting point is a family of planes in R3:
y=Yθ​(η,ξ)=η(cosθ,sinθ,0)+ξ(0,0,1).
They cover all values of y. On each plane, the matrix Q(y) has a Gram factorization linear in (η,ξ) and trigonometric of degree three in θ. This gives a 20×20 linear pencil Lθ​ whose positive semidefinite locus is exactly the corresponding slice of K, including its boundary.
The angular parameter does not itself furnish a finite linear matrix inequality. We instead introduce a real linear functional on a finite-dimensional space of trigonometric polynomials with coefficients linear in the slice variables. We require it to be nonnegative on qTLθ​q for every vector q of trigonometric polynomials of degree at most two. These requirements form one finite matrix inequality. Evaluation at a single angle provides a feasible functional for every point of K.
This use of a finite matrix to encode positivity against a space of test polynomials belongs to the moment and sum-of-squares approach to semidefinite representations [Las01; Las09]. Here exactness must hold at one fixed degree.
The main issue is the converse: an arbitrary feasible functional need not be evaluation at an angle, or integration against a measure. The degree-two matching identity in Section 3 supplies enough test vectors to recover the matrix inequalities defining each slice. Its construction rotates a fixed complex Gram factor by a 2×2 unitary matrix. The rotation preserves the Gram matrix and reduces a cubic trigonometric pairing to a first harmonic. Matching its value and first derivative then identifies the pairing exactly. This bounded-degree construction is the principal additional algebraic ingredient of the lift. Section 4 applies it to prove exactness for every feasible functional and completes the proof of Theorem 1.1.

2 Exact semidefinite representations on angular slices

We first construct a matrix pencil on each plane y=Yθ​(η,ξ). Its determinant will agree with p on that plane. This will identify cone membership with positive semidefiniteness even when X is singular.
For θ∈R, set
c=cosθ,s=sinθ,w=eiθ,d(θ)=(c,s,0),k=(0,0,1),
and write
Yθ​(η,ξ)=ηd(θ)+ξk(η,ξ∈R).
These planes cover R3. We first factor Q on each plane, using complex notation to keep the formulas short. For a complex matrix F=(f1​,f2​)∈C3×2, define its realification by
F=(Ref1​,Imf1​,Ref2​,Imf2​).
Thus FFT=Re(FF∗), where ∗ denotes conjugate transpose. Define
U(θ)=2​1​​−w−1sw−2cw−2​−wsw2−cw2​​,V0​=2​1​​0i1​0i1​​,Fθ​(η,ξ)=ηU(θ)+ξV0​.(4)
Lemma 2.1 (Angular Gram factorization).
For every θ,η,ξ∈R,
Fθ​(η,ξ)Fθ​(η,ξ)T=Q(Yθ​(η,ξ)).(5)
In particular, Q(y)⪰0 for every y∈R3.
Proof.
The three coefficients in the quadratic expansion of Re(Fθ​Fθ∗​) are
Re(UU∗)Re(UV0∗​+V0​U∗)​=​1−sc0​−scs20​00c2​​,=​00−c​00−s​−c−s0​​.​Re(V0​V0∗​)=​000​010​001​​,
For the (2,3) entry of the last matrix, the multiplication gives scos(2θ)−csin(2θ)=−s. The sum of these matrices with coefficients η2,ξ2,ηξ is exactly Q(ηc,ηs,ξ). Every real y has this form, so the factorization also proves positive semidefiniteness.
∎

2.1 The slice pencil

For a real column r∈R3 and a real vector u=(u0​,u′)∈R×R3, define
B(r)=(0−r​rT03×3​​),Ju​=(u′​−u0​I3​​).(6)
Then B(r)u=JuT​r. If r1​,…,r4​ are the columns of Fθ​(η,ξ), direct multiplication and Lemma 2.1 give
j=1∑4​B(rj​)TWB(rj​)=ΦYθ​(η,ξ)​(W)(W∈S4).(7)
Indeed, for W=(av​vTT​), the individual summands have blocks rjT​Trj​, −rjT​vrjT​, −rj​rjT​v, and arj​rjT​. Summing uses ∑j​rj​rjT​=Q(Yθ​(η,ξ)). Consequently, for every y∈R3,
uTΦy​(W)u=tr(Ju​WJuT​Q(y)).(8)
Here we used that the angular planes cover R3.
Write X,Z∈S4 for the matrix variables on a slice, and define
Lθ​(X,Z,η,ξ)=(I4​⊗XBθ​(η,ξ)T​Bθ​(η,ξ)Z​),Bθ​(η,ξ)=​B(r1​)B(r2​)B(r3​)B(r4​)​​.(9)
For fixed θ, this is a homogeneous real symmetric linear pencil of size twenty. Its coefficients are trigonometric polynomials in θ of degree at most three.
Lemma 2.2.
For every θ,η,ξ∈R and X,Z∈S4,
(X,Z,Yθ​(η,ξ))∈K⟺Lθ​(X,Z,η,ξ)⪰0.(10)
In particular, p is hyperbolic with respect to e. If X≻0, the conditions in (10) are also equivalent to Z⪰ΦYθ​(η,ξ)​(X−1).
Proof.
For invertible X, the block determinant formula and (7) show that
detLθ​​=(detX)4det(Z−ΦYθ​(η,ξ)​(X−1))=p(X,Z,Yθ​(η,ξ)).​
The second equality uses adjX=(detX)X−1 and linearity of Φy​ in its matrix argument. Both sides are polynomials in the slice variables, so the identity also holds for singular X. Moreover, Lθ​(I4​,I4​,0,0)=I20​. Thus
p(te−(X,Z,Yθ​(η,ξ)))=det(tI20​−Lθ​(X,Z,η,ξ)).(11)
The roots are the real eigenvalues of this symmetric pencil evaluated at the specified point. Since every y lies on some angular plane, this proves hyperbolicity. Nonnegativity of all these eigenvalues, including zero eigenvalues, proves (10). For X≻0, the final assertion is the Schur complement criterion applied to (9).
∎

3 A degree-two matching identity

Write
Q(y,z)=21​(Q(y+z)−Q(y)−Q(z))
for the symmetric bilinear polarization of Q, so that Q(y,y)=Q(y).
For S∈S3 and F,H∈C3×2, put
⟨F,H⟩S​=Retr(F∗SH)=tr(FTSH).
This is a symmetric real bilinear form. A complex trigonometric polynomial of degree at most j is a linear combination of eiℓθ for −j≤ℓ≤j.
The finite lift will test Lθ​ against trigonometric polynomial vectors built from the columns of a matrix C(θ). A constant Gram matrix for C makes the coefficient of X in the quadratic contribution of the top blocks independent of θ. Requiring ⟨Fθ​,C⟩S​=tr(SQ(Yθ​,z)) makes the mixed contribution linear in Yθ​. The next lemma achieves both properties with entries of degree at most two. The matrix S in the pairing may be indefinite.
Lemma 3.1 (Degree-two matching).
Let S∈S3 and let z∈R3 satisfy (z1​,z2​)=(0,0). There is a matrix C(θ)∈C3×2 whose entries are trigonometric polynomials of degree at most two such that, for all θ,η,ξ∈R,
C(θ)C(θ)T⟨Fθ​(η,ξ),C(θ)⟩S​​=Q(z),=tr(SQ(Yθ​(η,ξ),z)).​(12)
Proof.
Write z=τd(α)+ρk, where τ>0, and set
w0​=eiα,R0​=τU(α)+ρV0​,N=SR0​.
By Lemma 2.1, R0​R0T​=Q(z). We will set C(θ)=R0​M(θ) with M(θ) unitary, so that this Gram matrix remains fixed. We choose the rotation to make ⟨V0​,C⟩S​ constant and ⟨U(θ),C(θ)⟩S​ a linear combination of cosθ and sinθ. After those frequency bounds are established, values and a derivative at α will identify the pairings.
Choosing the unitary rotation. Write Nj​ for the jth row of N and introduce the two-component row
v=N3​−iN2​.
Subscripts + and − denote the first and second components of a row. Set
g=v+​+v−​​,h=v+​−v−​​,κ(θ)=(w0​/w)2,δ=∣g∣2+∣h∣2.
We seek a matrix of the form
M(θ)=(a−b​ba​).
Writing vM=vM, we impose the two conditions
v+M​+v−M​​=g,v+M​−v−M​​=hκ.(13)
The sum on the left controls the pairing with V0​, while the difference multiplies w3 in the pairing with U. These conditions therefore keep the first pairing constant and lower the cubic term of the second to frequency one, since w3κ=w02​w. The expansion below will also bound its remaining frequencies.
The two left sides of (13) are ga+hb and ha−g​b, respectively. Thus, for δ>0, we choose a(θ) and b(θ) by solving
(gh​h−g​​)(ab​)=(ghκ​).(14)
The coefficient matrix A satisfies A∗A=δI2​, so the system has a unique solution. Explicitly,
a=δ∣g∣2+∣h∣2κ​,b=δgh(1−κ)​.(15)
Since the right side of (14) has squared norm δ, we have ∣a∣2+∣b∣2=1. For δ=0, take a=1 and b=0; then g=h=0 and the same system is satisfied. In both cases M is unitary, M(α)=I2​, and a,b involve only the frequencies 0 and −2. Thus C=R0​M has degree at most two and C(α)=R0​. Moreover,
CCT=Re(R0​MM∗R0∗​)=Re(R0​R0∗​)=Q(z),
which proves the first identity in (12).
Reducing the frequencies of the pairings. The formula for V0​ and (13) yield
2​⟨V0​,C⟩S​=Re(v+M​+v−M​)=Reg,
so this pairing is constant.
Set m=N3​+iN2​, n=N1​, and write mM=mM, nM=nM. Expanding c and s in powers of w, the formula for U gives
2​⟨U(θ),C(θ)⟩S​=Re[​21​w3v+M​+w(21​m+M​−n+M​)−21​w−3v−M​+w−1(−21​m−M​−n−M​)].​
Inside the real part, we may replace each negative-power term by its complex conjugate. The resulting expression is
Re[2w3​(v+M​−v−M​​)+w(2m+M​​−n+M​−2m−M​​​−n−M​​)].(16)
The first term has frequency one because w3κ=w02​w. In the second term, the expression in parentheses has only frequencies 0 and −2: for any fixed row r,
(rM)+​=r+​a−r−​b,(rM)−​​=r+​​b+r−​​a.
Consequently (16) is a real linear combination of cosθ and sinθ, as required.
Identifying the pairings. At θ=α, polarization of Lemma 2.1 within the plane spanned by d(α) and k gives
⟨V0​,R0​⟩S​⟨U(α),R0​⟩S​​=tr(SQ(k,z)),=tr(SQ(d(α),z)).​(17)(18)​
Both sides of the desired identity ⟨V0​,C(θ)⟩S​=tr(SQ(k,z)) are constant, so (17) proves it for every θ.
For the pairing with U, both ⟨U(θ),C(θ)⟩S​ and tr(SQ(d(θ),z)) are linear combinations of cosθ and sinθ. They agree at α by (18); it remains to compare their derivatives there. The fixed Gram matrix of C gives
⟨C(θ),C(θ)⟩S​=tr(SQ(z)),⟨R0​,C′(α)⟩S​=0.
Constancy of the pairing with V0​ also gives ⟨V0​,C′(α)⟩S​=0. Since R0​=τU(α)+ρV0​ and τ>0, it follows that
⟨U(α),C′(α)⟩S​=0.(19)
Next differentiate the identity
⟨τU(θ)+ρV0​,τU(θ)+ρV0​⟩S​=tr(SQ(τd(θ)+ρk)),
which follows from Lemma 2.1. Evaluating at α and dividing by 2τ gives
⟨U′(α),R0​⟩S​=tr(SQ(d′(α),z)).
Together with (19), this is the required derivative identity. A real linear combination of cosθ and sinθ is determined by its value and derivative at a single angle. Hence the pairing with U has the desired value for all θ. Linearity in η,ξ completes the proof.
∎

4 A finite semidefinite lift

We now replace the angular family of pencils by one finite matrix condition. Evaluation on an angular slice will provide a feasible lift for each point of K. Conversely, the functions supplied by Lemma 3.1 will turn positivity of the finite matrix into the inequalities that characterize the slice, including its singular boundary.

4.1 The matrix condition

Let Tj​ be the real vector space of trigonometric polynomials of degree at most j, with basis
1,cosθ,sinθ,…,cos(jθ),sin(jθ).
Let E be the space of real functions of (θ,X,Z,η,ξ) that are linear homogeneous in the 22 coordinates of (X,Z,η,ξ)∈S4×S4×R2, with coefficients in T7​. Thus dimE=22⋅15=330. Our lifting variable is a real linear functional Λ:E→R; on vectors and matrices we apply it entrywise. For an output point (X,Z,y), impose
Λ(X)=X,Λ(Z)=Z,Λ(Yθ​(η,ξ))=y.(20)
We also require
Λ(q(θ)TLθ​(X,Z,η,ξ)q(θ))≥0for every q∈(T2​)20.(21)
The expression to which Λ is applied lies in E: the entries of Lθ​ have trigonometric degree at most three, so its product with two entries of q has degree at most seven.
Condition (21) is a single finite semidefinite condition, using the finite test-space construction familiar from moment relaxations [Las01; Las09]. Indeed, set (f1​,…,f5​)=(1,cosθ,sinθ,cos2θ,sin2θ) and define H(Λ)∈S100 by
H(Λ)(i,a),(j,b)​=Λ(fa​fb​(Lθ​)ij​),1≤i,j≤20,1≤a,b≤5.(22)
If qi​=∑a​ti,a​fa​, the left side of (21) is tTH(Λ)t. Hence (21) is equivalent to H(Λ)⪰0. Every entry of this real symmetric matrix is linear homogeneous in the 330 coordinates of Λ.
Proposition 4.1.
For (X,Z,y)∈S4×S4×R3, the following are equivalent:
  1. (X,Z,y)∈K;
  2. there is a real linear functional Λ:E→R satisfying (20) and H(Λ)⪰0.
Proof.
Suppose first that (X,Z,y)∈K. Choose θ0​,η0​,ξ0​ with y=Yθ0​​(η0​,ξ0​), and let Λ be evaluation at (θ0​,X,Z,η0​,ξ0​). The output equations hold, and Lemma 2.2 gives Lθ0​​(X,Z,η0​,ξ0​)⪰0, which implies (21). This evaluation functional is a finite feasible witness even when X is singular.
For the converse, suppose that Λ satisfies the stated conditions. Taking constant q supported on one of the four top blocks of Lθ​ in (21) gives X⪰0. We next obtain a family of scalar inequalities from which the remaining slice conditions will follow.
Fix u∈R4, D∈S4, and z∈R3 with (z1​,z2​)=(0,0), and apply Lemma 3.1 with S=Ju​DJuT​∈S3. Neither D nor S is required to be positive semidefinite. Let b1​(θ),…,b4​(θ) be the columns of the resulting real matrix C(θ). Choose the five four-dimensional blocks of q to be
q(θ)=​−DJuT​b1​(θ)⋮−DJuT​b4​(θ)u​​.
The degree bound in Lemma 3.1 puts this vector in (T2​)20. Write rj​ for the columns of Fθ​(η,ξ), as in the definition of Lθ​. Using B(rj​)u=JuT​rj​, the top blocks and the cross terms of qTLθ​q are respectively
j=1∑4​bjT​Ju​DXDJuT​bj​−2j=1∑4​bjT​Ju​DJuT​rj​​=tr(Ju​DXDJuT​Q(z)),=−2⟨Fθ​(η,ξ),C(θ)⟩S​=−2tr(Ju​DJuT​Q(Yθ​(η,ξ),z)).​
These identities hold before applying Λ. The first identity removes the angular dependence from the coefficient of X; the last expression is linear in Yθ​(η,ξ). Consequently, applying (20) and (21) gives
uTZu+tr(Ju​DXDJuT​Q(z))−2tr(Ju​DJuT​Q(y,z))≥0.(23)
For fixed u,D, the left side is a polynomial in z, so the inequality extends by continuity to every z∈R3. Only this scalar inequality is extended; no continuity of the functions C is needed. Thus (23) holds for all u∈R4, D∈S4, and z∈R3.
If X were positive definite, setting z=y and D=X−1 in (23) would give Z⪰Φy​(X−1). For singular X, the same family of tests also supplies the necessary range condition. Fix slice parameters y=Yθ0​​(η0​,ξ0​) and, for the rest of the proof, let rj​ denote the columns of Fθ0​​(η0​,ξ0​) and set Bj​=B(rj​). For v∈kerX, take D=tvvT and z=y in (23), where t∈R is arbitrary. Since DXD=0, this gives
uTZu−2t(Ju​v)TQ(y)(Ju​v)≥0(t∈R).
Its coefficient of t must vanish. The Gram factorization of Q(y) therefore yields
0=(Ju​v)TQ(y)(Ju​v)=j=1∑4​(vTBj​u)2.
As u and v∈kerX are arbitrary, it follows that
rangeBj​⊆(kerX)⊥=rangeX(1≤j≤4).(24)
Let X† be the symmetric matrix that inverts the positive eigenvalues of X and is zero on kerX. In particular, X†XX†=X†. Taking D=X† and z=y in (23), and using (8) and (7), gives
Z⪰Φy​(X†)=j=1∑4​BjT​X†Bj​.(25)
We now verify positivity of the slice pencil directly by completing a square using (24) and (25). For a1​,…,a4​,u∈R4, its quadratic form equals
​j=1∑4​ajT​Xaj​+2j=1∑4​ajT​Bj​u+uTZu=j=1∑4​(aj​+X†Bj​u)TX(aj​+X†Bj​u)+uT(Z−j=1∑4​BjT​X†Bj​)u≥0.​
Here the cross terms agree because XX†Bj​=Bj​ by (24). Thus Lθ0​​(X,Z,η0​,ξ0​)⪰0, and Lemma 2.2 gives (X,Z,y)∈K.
∎
The converse has used an arbitrary feasible functional Λ. In particular, the proof requires no representation of Λ by a measure and no closure operation on the projected feasible set.

4.2 The size of the lift

Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Choose the displayed trigonometric basis of T7​ and the upper-triangular coordinate functions of X and Z, together with η,ξ, to specify the 330 coordinates of Λ. The output equations (20) prescribe precisely the following 23 distinct coordinates:
Λ(Xij​),Λ(Zij​)(1≤i≤j≤4),Λ(ηcosθ),Λ(ηsinθ),Λ(ξ).​
They are independent members of the chosen coordinate system on E∗. Substitute the corresponding entries of X,Z,y for these coordinates in (22), and use the remaining 330−23=307 coordinates as auxiliary variables. The result is a fixed real symmetric 100×100 matrix pencil, homogeneous in the output and auxiliary variables. Proposition 4.1 proves that its projection is exactly K. Hence the requested representation has N=100, m=307, and zero constant term.
∎
